summary: GitHub is about as friendly as OAuth gets. Create an OAuth App and it works for any GitHub user straight away - no review, no verification, no waiting. The one real decision is whether you need an OAuth App or a GitHub App, because they are different things.

rationale: No approval or review gate for OAuth Apps.
The flow is the textbook authorization-code grant with solid docs.
The main trap is conceptual: OAuth App vs GitHub App.

timeEstimate.setup: 15 to 30 minutes from nothing to a working sign-in.

basis.text: GitHub's own docs describe no review step for OAuth Apps.

steps.title: Register the OAuth App
steps.detail: GitHub > Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps > New OAuth App. Set the homepage URL and the authorization callback URL.

steps.title: Copy the client ID and secret
steps.detail: Generate a client secret on the app page and keep it in your server environment, never in the browser or the repo.

steps.title: Run the flow
steps.detail: Send users to github.com/login/oauth/authorize with your client ID and scopes, then exchange the returned code for a token. Done.

requirements.item: A callback URL for your app (localhost works fine for development)

gotchas.text: An OAuth App always acts as the user who authorized it. If you need the app to act on its own (bot comments, installation tokens), you want a GitHub App instead.
Unverified OAuth Apps hit a limit of 50 new authorizations per hour - a problem only once you have real traffic.
You can't see a client secret again after leaving the page; store it when you create it.

agentCanDo: Keep this guide synced with GitHub's docs
Help decide OAuth App vs GitHub App from your feature list
List the scopes your API calls need
developerMustDo: Register the app under their own GitHub account
Choose scopes and implement token storage
